summary: This standards-track RFC specifies a Management Information Base for the Operations, Administration, and Maintenance objects of TRILL, so that network management tools can monitor and configure those functions using SNMP.

plainLanguage.summary: A MIB is a standard list of dials and gauges on a device. This lists the ones used to check on and look after a TRILL network.

questions: what is the trill oam mib
snmp objects for trill path trace
what is a mep in trill
subtitle: The SNMP management objects for monitoring and driving TRILL fault-management tests such as path trace.

tldr.problem: TRILL has an OAM framework and a fault-management solution (RFC 7455), but operators need a standard way to configure those tests and read their results over SNMP.
tldr.mechanism: The TRILL-OAM-MIB module augments the Ethernet CFM MIB tables with TRILL objects and adds tables for flow configuration, path trace replies and multi-destination tree verification replies.
tldr.outcome: Management systems can run and read TRILL path traces and tree checks, and receive a fault alarm when a MEP loses or regains contact with a peer flow.

today: RFC 7784 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is the initial version of the TRILL OAM MIB, as its own revision text states.

sections.title: Where This MIB Fits
sections.content:
TRILL OAM (Operations, Administration, and Maintenance) meets the requirements of RFC 6905. Its general framework is in RFC 7174, and the fault-management details are in RFC 7455, which reuses the message format of Ethernet Connectivity Fault Management (CFM) from IEEE 802.1Q.

This document does the same for management. It uses the CFM MIB modules as a base, augments their existing tables with TRILL objects, and adds a new table for TRILL-specific capabilities. The module follows the Internet-Standard Management Framework: objects live in a Management Information Base (MIB), are written in SMIv2, and are normally accessed with SNMP.
sections.plainLanguage: TRILL already knows how to test itself. This document is the list of buttons and meters that let a person see those tests from a management program.

sections.title: Structure of the MIB Module
sections.content:
The module has a notifications subtree, trillOamNotifications, and an objects subtree, trillOamMibObjects, with conformance information alongside. Under the objects sit five tables, all in the trillOamMep group.

  • trillOamMepTable augments dot1agCfmMepEntry and holds local TRILL OAM settings and counters per MEP (Maintenance End Point). Rows appear and disappear with the underlying CFM rows.
  • trillOamMepFlowCfgTable holds one row per configured flow on a MEP.
  • trillOamPtrTable holds Path Trace Reply entries.
  • trillOamMtvrTable holds Multi-destination Tree Verification Reply entries.
  • trillOamMepDbTable augments dot1agCfmMepDbTable with per-flow state for remote MEPs.

The module is registered as { mib-2 238 }.
sections.plainLanguage: The MIB is like a filing cabinet with five drawers: one for each device's own settings, one for the flows being tested, two for answers that come back, and one for what is known about the other end.

sections.title: Flows, Path Traces and Tree Checks
sections.content:
A flow is described by a row in the flow configuration table, indexed by Maintenance Domain, MANET, MEP and a flow index (1 to 65535). Each row has 96 bytes of flow entropy, a target destination RBridge nickname and a hop count (1 to 63). A row is managed with a RowStatus object, and all columns MUST have a valid value before it can be activated.

The MEP table carries the transmit settings for loopback, Path Trace Messages (PTM, for unicast paths) and Multi-destination Tree Verification Messages (MTVM, for multicast trees). These include destination, hop count, whether the reply is in or out of band, and the flow entropy. It also keeps counters of replies received, received out of order, and sent.

Replies are stored in the Path Trace Reply table, indexed by transaction identifier, and in the Multi-destination Reply table, which adds the receive order of replies. Entries record details such as the ingress and egress ports and the next-hop nicknames.
sections.plainLanguage: To test a road, you pick a route and send a scout. The scout's reports are written down in order so the manager can read them later.

sections.title: Relationship to the CFM and LLDP MIBs
sections.content:
Objects already defined in IEEE8021-CFM-MIB and LLDP-MIB are not duplicated. The module imports index and type objects from them, and implementing IEEE8021-CFM-MIB is required because the TRILL tables augment its tables. Objects that do not apply to TRILL must be handled by the implementation, which returns the default values described in the CFM MIB.

For labels, TRILL can use a 12-bit VLAN or a 24-bit Fine-Grained Label (RFC 7172). The module reuses value 2 of the IEEE8021 service selector type, which represents a 24-bit isid, for TRILL's Fine-Grained Label.

TRILL OAM does not support the Link Trace Message or Reply. As described in RFC 7455, Path Trace and Multi-destination Tree Verification take their place, and statistics for the Link Trace messages should default as in the CFM MIB.
sections.plainLanguage: This MIB borrows from existing lists instead of copying them. Where TRILL does something differently, it says so and uses its own tools.

sections.title: Fault Alarm Notification
sections.content:
The one notification is trillOamFaultAlarm. It is sent to the management entity whenever a MEP loses or restores contact with its peer flow MEPs, and it reports the flow state (trillOamMepDbFlowState). The receiver identifies the system from the notification's source address and the flow from the indices in the object identifier: Maintenance Domain, Maintenance Association, MEP identifier and flow index.

The per-flow state of each remote MEP is kept in the MEP database table, together with the time it last entered a failed or OK state, the remote RBridge nickname and the last sequence number received.
sections.plainLanguage: When a device stops hearing from a partner it was checking on, it rings an alarm bell. The bell also says which partner and which check went quiet.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Improper manipulation of these objects may cause denial of service to many end users. The read-create objects are the main concern. Three of them, trillOamMepTransmitLbmReplyIp, trillOamMepTransmitPtmReplyIp and trillOamMepTransmitMtvmReplyIp, let replies be sent to any IP address and can be used to attack that system. trillOamMepTxPtmMessages and trillOamMepTxMtvmMessages can generate lots of CPU-driven traffic on RBridges.

Readable objects can be sensitive as well: Path Trace messages expose the unicast topology, and Multi-destination Tree Verification Messages expose the multicast tree topology. Access should be controlled.

SNMP versions before SNMPv3 did not include adequate security, and deploying them is NOT RECOMMENDED. Implementations should provide the SNMPv3 security features, and those claiming SNMPv3 compliance MUST fully support authentication and privacy through the User-based Security Model with AES. IANA registered the module at { mib-2 238 }.
sections.plainLanguage: Some of the buttons could be used to make a device send floods of mail to a victim, and some of the meters reveal a map of the network. So only trusted people should be allowed to touch them.
